headline: Put a copy of a message's algorithm identifiers where its signature or its MAC covers them, and refuse one whose copy disagrees.
summary: A CMS signature covers the algorithms it uses only indirectly, and an authenticated-data message does not cover them at all: RFC 5652 makes the MAC input the authenticated attributes alone, so the digest and MAC algorithm identifiers sit outside it. Rewriting the digest algorithm there leaves the MAC verifying and has the recipient recompute the content digest under the algorithm the attacker chose, which needs no key. `pki.cms.sign`, `pki.cms.countersign` and `pki.cms.authenticate` now emit the RFC 6211 CMSAlgorithmProtection attribute on request, a copy of those identifiers placed where the signature or the MAC covers them, and `pki.cms.verify` and `pki.cms.decrypt` compare every copy they find against the fields it protects. A disagreement is a refusal, which RFC 6211 requires of any verifier that reads the attribute at all.

Added: `algorithmProtection` on `pki.cms.sign`, `pki.cms.countersign` and `pki.cms.authenticate` emits the RFC 6211 `CMSAlgorithmProtection` attribute: a copy of the structure's digest algorithm identifier plus its signature algorithm identifier for a `SignerInfo` or its MAC algorithm identifier for an `AuthenticatedData`, each copied whole with its parameters from the value the field itself is built from. RFC 8933 section 4.1 makes including it a SHOULD, and RFC 9882 section 4 and RFC 9814 section 5 repeat that for ML-DSA and SLH-DSA, whose signatures carry no digest identifier of their own. It is off by default, because turning it on changes the bytes of every signature a caller emits. `true` writes the identifier RFC 6211 section 2 and Appendix A state, which OpenSSL registers as `id-aa-CMSAlgorithmProtection` and Bouncy Castle uses; `"registry"` writes the S/MIME arc value the IANA registry and `draft-ietf-lamps-rfc6211-update` give it.

`pki.cms.verify` compares the attribute against the fields it protects on every signer and every countersignature, and reports `algorithmProtection` per signer: `{ present, oid, compared, mismatch }`, where `compared` lists the identifiers actually checked. Both identifiers the attribute is assigned are read, because a verifier that recognizes one spelling and not the other checks nothing on a message using the other, which is the interop failure the update draft records between two shipped implementations. A disagreement fails the signer with `cms/algorithm-protection-mismatch`: section 3.1 makes both comparisons MUSTs once a validator supports the attribute. Both comparisons are modulo encoding, in the two ways section 3 names: a parameter field with an ASN.1 default compares the same written out as omitted, which that section makes a MUST and says a binary compare of the bytes cannot satisfy, and RSASSA-PSS is where it arises because RFC 4055 section 3.1 defaults all four of its fields; absent and DER NULL parameters read as one algorithm on the digest arm, which RFC 3370 section 2.1 and RFC 5754 section 2 require an implementation to accept. Anything else in a parameter field is read as written, since that is where RSASSA-PSS keeps its hash, mask generator, salt length and trailer field and the signature covers none of them. `requireAlgorithmProtection` turns an absent attribute into a failure for an operator whose profile asks for one, on every signer and on every countersignature at any depth.

`pki.cms.decrypt` compares the attribute on an `AuthenticatedData`, against the outer `digestAlgorithm` and `macAlgorithm` the MAC input does not cover, and reports the same `algorithmProtection` field on its result. The comparison runs before the MAC, because a mismatch is a statement about the message rather than about the key. `requireAlgorithmProtection` applies here too.

`pki.schema.cms.parseAlgorithmProtection(der)` decodes a `CMSAlgorithmProtection` value held on its own. A value carrying both arms, or neither, is refused `cms/bad-algorithm-protection-attr`, which is section 2's rule that exactly one of them is present; each failure says which. `pki.schema.cms.parse` decodes the attribute during its own walk, so a message carrying a malformed one, more than one value, more than one instance, or an instance in an unsigned, unauthenticated or unprotected position is refused there.

`pki.lint.cms` reports `lint/rfc8933/algorithm-protection-absent` as a notice on an originator that carries attributes and no such attribute. Section 4.1 states the requirement for both content types, so the row reads a `SignedData` signer's signed attributes and an `AuthenticatedData`'s authenticated attributes, the second being where the algorithm fields are covered by nothing at all. The SHOULD is conditioned on attributes being present, so an originator that signs or authenticates the content directly draws nothing. RFC 8933 updates RFC 5652 rather than restating it, so the row is its own profile: `pki.lint.cms(der, { profile: "rfc8933" })` asks only what that document added, `profile: "rfc5652"` asks only what that one states, and the default runs both. `pki.lint.profiles()` lists `rfc8933` alongside the rest.
Changed: Every verb that emits attributes refuses a caller-supplied algorithm protection attribute that this package's own verifier would then reject, with `cms/bad-input`. `pki.cms.sign`, `pki.cms.countersign` and `pki.cms.authenticate` refuse a copy contradicting the identifiers being emitted, a copy carrying more than one value, and a second one beside the attribute the verb itself emitted; caller-supplied attributes otherwise reach the wire unread. A copy that agrees is admitted. The attribute is refused in `unsignedAttributes`, which RFC 6211 section 2 forbids outright, and in an `AuthEnvelopedData`'s authenticated attributes, which RFC 8933 section 6 says it protects nothing in: that content type has no digest or MAC algorithm field for a copy to name. `pki.schema.cms.parse` refuses it in that set too, under either identifier, so a message from another producer is read by the same rule this package writes by; every restriction an authenticated-attribute set already carried still applies there, a countersignature among them. Which arm the value carries stays the validator's question: RFC 6211 section 2 says which arm a producer fills and sections 3.1 and 3.2 give the consequence to whoever validates, so a message holding the other arm parses, to be read, and `pki.cms.verify` or `pki.cms.decrypt` refuses it as the mismatch it is. Asking for `algorithmProtection` together with `signedAttributes: false` is refused, since the attribute rides in the signed attributes and a message cannot carry it without them, and so is asking for it with `authenticatedAttributes: false`, where the MAC covers the content octets directly and no attribute set is built. The off forms stay accepted in both of those modes: a caller passing one options object to several messages does not have to strip a switch it had already turned off.
A verified countersignature row carries one more field, `algorithmProtection`, beside `ok`, `sid`, `cert`, `digestAlgorithm`, `unsignedAttrs` and `countersignatures`.

An option that turns a check on is read as the boolean it documents, and any other value is refused at the door with the module's `bad-input` code. This covers `requireAlgorithmProtection` on `pki.cms.verify` and `pki.cms.decrypt`, `requireRevocation` and the RFC 5280 section 6.1.1 policy inputs `initialExplicitPolicy`, `initialAnyPolicyInhibit` and `initialPolicyMappingInhibit` on `pki.path.validate`, `requireJsonContentType` on `pki.ct.fetchLogList`, and `expectSCEPStandard` and `requireStrongProfile` on `pki.scep.getCACaps`. The off forms are `false`, `null` and an absent option; every other value is refused, in both directions. A `"true"` read out of a config file is unequal to `true`, and a boundary comparing against `true` ran with the check disabled, while a truthiness test turned one on for `"false"`. A trust anchor's own copies of those three policy flags were already typed where they are copied, and a caller's values are compared against them. `algorithmProtection` takes `true`, `"registry"`, `false`, `null` or an absent option, and refuses every other value.

Each of those options is typed before the thing it governs happens, and the value that passed is the value the check uses. `pki.path.build` types the four switches it forwards, and its own `validate`, at its own door, because a build reaches an AIA fetch before it reaches `pki.path.validate` and a build that assembles no path never calls it. Normalizing a trust anchor reads its name, key and algorithm, and those reads run caller code when the anchor carries accessors, so the typed values are what each anchor attempt is handed rather than whatever an options object the caller still holds says by then. `pki.cms.verify` reads its policy switches ahead of deriving the message and copying the trust material for the same reason. `pki.cms.sign`, `pki.cms.countersign` and `pki.cms.authenticate` resolve `algorithmProtection` at their own door as well: signing an async iterable hashes the stream to build the attributes, and a value refused only there is refused after the stream has been drained, which a caller cannot act on for an input that cannot be replayed and never arrives at all for one that does not end; `pki.cms.authenticate` likewise refuses before it hashes the content and wraps each recipient's key. `pki.path.build` refuses `requireRevocation` or any of the three policy inputs asked for together with `validate: false`, which returns the ordered path without validating and so applies none of them.

`pki.cms.decrypt` refuses `requireAlgorithmProtection` on a content type that cannot carry the attribute. RFC 8933 section 6 gives it a place in an `AuthenticatedData` alone, so an `EnvelopedData`, `AuthEnvelopedData` or `EncryptedData` cannot satisfy the requirement, and the plaintext came back before without the requirement having been applied or reported. The refusal is `cms/bad-input` and names the content type.
